15: ---

17: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
18:

28: ## 2. OVERVIEW
29: 
30: ### Purpose
31: 
32: Code work is not one activity. Writing code needs author-side quality gates and comment hygiene. Reviewing it needs a findings-first baseline with security and correctness checks. CI workflow work needs trigger, permission and job-shape rules. System work needs hook and alignment verification. Each kind of code work carries its own contract, yet they all share the same surface identity rules.
33: 
34: Without one routing point, every contract would duplicate surface detection and a request that touches several kinds of code work would have no ordered way to resolve. sk-code exists so one advisor identity covers the whole code family: the hub centralizes surface detection once and routes each request to the focused packet that owns the work.
35: 
36: ### When to Use
37: 
38: Reach for sk-code when the task is code work and the next step is implementation, author-side quality, debugging, verification or review. Shared stack detection tries every declared specific surface first, then the SKILLED fallback, then UNKNOWN. A skill outside the hub that names family sk-code can declare its own `surface_detection` block in `graph-metadata.json` and outrank SKILLED. The CI surface is bundled from request vocabulary, not from detection (see `shared/references/stack-detection.md`). Use a mode hint when you already know the contract you need and let the hub classify when the request spans intents.
39: 
40: ### What It Does
41: 
42: `Skill(sk-code)` loads the hub. The hub routes the request through `mode-registry.json` to one of two workflow modes. Root `ROUTER.md` then selects the packet leaves and declared shared controls bundled alongside it. Each mode and surface holds its own code-work contract while the hub itself stays routing-only. The packets carry no `graph-metadata.json`, so the advisor discovers exactly one code skill.

123: - **Frontend** (`.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-frontend/`): stack-agnostic web practice, topic references and Figma-to-code checks.
124: - **Skilled** (`.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-skilled/`): the native standards for this framework's own code, so keep it.
125: 
126: A surface you add for your own stack ranks ahead of the Skilled surface. Run every command below from the repository root.
127: 
128: ### Before You Start
129: 
130: 1. In a fresh clone, run `bash .skilled/skills/sk-git/scripts/worktree-naming.sh provision .` first. It installs the dependencies and builds the spec-kit outputs the checks below load. Without it, `parent-skill-check.cjs` and `ci-skill-root-metadata.cjs` fail on a missing `@spec-kit/shared` build.
131: 2. In a clone, run `git config --local skilled.trustRepoHooks true` before you install the hooks. The hooks run this repository's scripts only in a trusted clone, so without it the commit-time re-mint never fires.
132: 3. Install the git hooks with `bash .skilled/scripts/install-git-hooks.sh`. A commit that stages the hub's routing files then re-mints its activation manifest and copies the manifest to its authored path. Without the hooks, do both by hand after each routing change: run `node .skilled/bin/compiled-route-manifest.cjs refresh --hub sk-code --skill-root .skilled/skills/sk-code`, then copy `.skilled/bin/lib/compiled-routing/013-live-activation/activation/sk-code/manifest.json` over `specs/sk-doc/z_archive/019-skill-routing-refactor/015-router-unification-program/013-live-activation/activation/sk-code/manifest.json`.
133: 4. If you prune `specs/`, keep `specs/sk-doc/z_archive/019-skill-routing-refactor/015-router-unification-program/`, the authored source of compiled routing, and keep the `.opencode/skills` link. Without either one the guard and sync checks fail.
134:

136:

138:

140: 2. In `.skilled/skills/sk-code/mode-registry.json`, delete the mode's `modes` entry and its name in `extensions.surface-axis.surfaces`. In `.skilled/skills/sk-code/hub-router.json`, delete it from `routerPolicy.tieBreak`, delete its `routerSignals` entry and delete the two `vocabularyClasses` that entry names.
141: 3. Regenerate the leaf manifest with `node .skilled/skills/sk-doc/sk-create-skill/scripts/generate-leaf-manifest.cjs --write .skilled/skills/sk-code`.
142: 4. Edit section 8 of `.skilled/skills/sk-code/ROUTER.md` by hand, because no command writes it. Delete every `RESOURCE_MAP` path under `<mode>/`, then delete each key left with no paths from both `RESOURCE_MAP` and `INTENT_SIGNALS`. Trim the prose map rows and sections above section 8 that point at the removed packet.
143: 5. Update the surface table and the surface list sentence in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/SKILL.md`, the mode's `surfaceDetection` block in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/mode-registry.json` (`stack-detection.md` section 2 reads it) and the surface lines in the root `README.md`.
144: 6. Delete or adjust the files written for the surface. These are its scenarios under `.skilled/skills/sk-code/manual-testing-playbook/`, with their rows in `manual-testing-playbook.md`, the surface checklist pointers in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-quality/`, the entries in `.skilled/skills/sk-code/feature-catalog/feature-catalog.md` and `.skilled/skills/sk-code/feature-catalog/two-axis-registry-driven-routing/two-axis-registry-driven-routing.md`, which name each live surface, the cases in `.skilled/bin/tests/compiled-route-surface-hint.test.cjs` and the canary cases that name the mode in `.skilled/bin/lib/compiled-routing/009-parent-hub-rollout/001-sk-code/fixtures/canary-cases.v1.json`. 149: ### Add Your Own Surface
150: 
151: 1. Run `/create:skill-parent update --surfaces <name>` in your AI runtime. Its steps live in `.skilled/commands/create/assets/create-skill-parent-auto.yaml`. It scaffolds the packet, registers it and places it ahead of `sk-code-skilled` in `tieBreak`, so your surface wins a keyword tie. If you edit `tieBreak` by hand instead, keep your surface ahead of `sk-code-skilled`, because the doctor's check 5l warns about a surface placed after it, and the registry compiler rejects a hub whose single fallback is not ranked last in `routerPolicy.tieBreak` (`SURFACE_FALLBACK_INVALID`).

158: 
159: A surface you keep out of the repository lives in its own skill beside the hub instead of inside it.

68: ## 4. SHARED WORKFLOW DOCTRINE
69: 
70: Implement, debug and verify are phases, not modes. Their doctrine is surface-agnostic and lives once here. Each surface packet reaches it through symlinks, so the active surface carries the full workflow without a forked copy:
71: 
72: ```text
73: ../sk-code-ci/references/workflow-implement.md       -> ./references/workflow-implement.md
74: ../sk-code-ci/references/workflow-debug.md           -> ./references/workflow-debug.md
75: ../sk-code-ci/references/workflow-verify.md          -> ./references/workflow-verify.md
76: ../sk-code-frontend/references/workflow-implement.md -> ./references/workflow-implement.md
77: ../sk-code-frontend/references/workflow-debug.md     -> ./references/workflow-debug.md
78: ../sk-code-frontend/references/workflow-verify.md    -> ./references/workflow-verify.md
79: ../sk-code-skilled/references/workflow-implement.md  -> ./references/workflow-implement.md
80: ../sk-code-skilled/references/workflow-debug.md      -> ./references/workflow-debug.md
81: ../sk-code-skilled/references/workflow-verify.md     -> ./references/workflow-verify.md
82: ```
83: 
84: Paths are relative to this folder. On disk each link is the relative target `../../shared/references/workflow-<phase>.md`.
85: 
86: | File | Purpose | Read by |
87: |---|---|---|
88: | [`references/workflow-implement.md`](./references/workflow-implement.md) | Research and mutating build work after the router resolves the active surface | All three surface packets through their symlinks, `../SKILL.md` |
89: | [`references/workflow-debug.md`](./references/workflow-debug.md) | Root-cause diagnosis and scoped repair after a symptom, failing command, runtime error or failed gate, plus the command-failure recovery order | All three surfaces, `../ROUTER.md` with the DEBUGGING intent, hand-offs from `sk-code-quality` and `sk-code-review` |
90: | [`references/workflow-verify.md`](./references/workflow-verify.md) | The non-mutating evidence phase that runs last, compares against a baseline and gates any done, works, fixed or passing claim | All three surfaces, `../ROUTER.md` with the VERIFICATION intent, hand-offs from both workflow modes, the `sk-code-review` rule-copy check |
91: 
92: Edit the file under [`./references/`](./references/). A symlink resolves to it, so a change here reaches every surface at once.

96: ## 5. UNIVERSAL STANDARDS
97: 
98: | File | Purpose | Read by |
99: |---|---|---|
100: | [`references/universal/code-quality-standards.md`](./references/universal/code-quality-standards.md) | The stack-agnostic P0/P1/P2 severity model for the Phase 1.5 Code Quality Gate, with an id and a FIXED or overridable mark on each floor rule | `sk-code-quality` before any implementation-done claim, the `../ROUTER.md` preamble, the `sk-code-review` rule-copy check |
101: | [`references/universal/rule-overrides.md`](./references/universal/rule-overrides.md) | The shared contract for a checklist's optional `## Rule overrides` section: row format, rule ids, the hard floor, precedence and how an override is recorded. The floor ids live once in [`references/universal/rule-overrides.json`](./references/universal/rule-overrides.json) | `sk-code-quality`, `sk-code-review`, which adopts it in `review-core.md` section 8, and the linter below |
102: | [`scripts/check-rule-overrides.cjs`](./scripts/check-rule-overrides.cjs) | Checks a checklist's override section, refuses any floor id and is the only path a mode reads a section through. Run `node --test .skilled/skills/sk-code/shared/scripts/tests/check-rule-overrides.test.cjs` for its suite. `review-lens-overrides.test.cjs` checks the review mode's floor and lens ids, its TODO rule's hygiene mapping and the SKILLED surface rows against the contract | Authors of a checklist with an override section, `sk-code-quality` through `--explain` and in every run, and `sk-code-review`, which reads the rows the resolver returns |
103: | [`scripts/lib/rule-registry.cjs`](./scripts/lib/rule-registry.cjs) | Reads every rule id an override row may name from the three documents that declare them: the runner's ids from `runner-contract.md` section 5, the `floor.*` ids from `code-quality-standards.md` and the `review.*` ids from `review-core.md` section 8. A missing table, or a table row that names no id, throws with its file, so the registry cannot shrink unnoticed. Run `node --test .skilled/skills/sk-code/shared/scripts/tests/rule-registry.test.cjs` for its suite | The quality runner, which refuses a row whose id is unknown, and the doctor status |

108: 
109: ## 6. WHAT BELONGS HERE
110: 
111: A file belongs in `shared/` only when it is doctrine about the parent hub or about how its nested modes work together. Surface detection, the phase lifecycle, the cross-surface workflow doctrine, the cross-mode severity model and the rule override contract both modes read pass that test.
112: 
113: A file stays out of `shared/` when a single mode or surface owns it:
114: 
115: - A mode's checklists, style guides and recovery playbooks go in that mode's own references or assets folder.
116: - Stack-specific standards go in the surface packet that owns the stack.
117: - Per-mode workflow contracts never land here, and neither does graph metadata. The hub carries the only [`../graph-metadata.json`](../graph-metadata.json).
118: 
119: When a shared file turns out to serve a single mode, move it into that mode and update its readers.
120:

13: 
14: # Phase Detection and Lifecycle
15: 
16: Every sk-code task that changes code moves through the same gated phases, from research to verified completion. Open it when the next move is unclear: which phase a task is in, which doctrine owns it, or what evidence ends it.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose
23: 
24: Keep research, implementation, the quality gate, debugging and verification in a fixed order, so no task reaches "done" on a skipped gate. The active surface changes which resources and evidence each phase uses. It never changes the order or the gates.
25: 
26: ### When to Use
27: 
28: - Planning code work on any sk-code surface.
29: - Choosing which phase doctrine and checklists to load next.
30: - Routing a failed quality or verification gate back to debugging or implementation.
31: - Judging whether the completion evidence is enough to claim "done".
32: 
33: ### Core Principle
34: 
35: A phase ends on evidence, not on effort. The next phase starts only when the current one has produced what its exit condition names.
36: 
37: ### Key Sources
38: 
39: - [stack-detection.md](./stack-detection.md) selects the surface. It returns SKILLED or UNKNOWN and never `sk-code-ci` or `sk-code-frontend`, which the hub bundles from request vocabulary alone (`code-ci-aliases` and `code-ci-runtime`, and `code-frontend-aliases`, in `hub-router.json`).
40: - `mode-registry.json` declares the workflow modes (`sk-code-quality`, `sk-code-review`) and the surfaces (`sk-code-ci`, `sk-code-frontend`, `sk-code-skilled`).
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 2. PHASE MAP
45: 
46: ```text
47: Phase 0   Research        optional for simple edits, required for complex or risky work
48: Phase 1   Implementation
49: Phase 1.5 Code Quality Gate
50: Phase 2   Debugging       entered when a check fails
51: Phase 3   Verification
52: done      only with recorded verification evidence
53: ```
54: 
55: Implement, debug and verify are not modes. Their doctrine lives once in `shared/references/workflow-*.md`, and each surface reaches it through a symlink in its own `references/` folder.
56: 
57: | Phase | Owner | What the phase produces |
58: | --- | --- | --- |
59: | 0 Research | [workflow-implement.md](./workflow-implement.md) §2 Research | Target files read, every place the change must reach listed, a plan |
60: | 1 Implementation | [workflow-implement.md](./workflow-implement.md) | The smallest correct change, plus a baseline and blast-radius note |
61: | 1.5 Code Quality Gate | `sk-code-quality` mode, [code-quality-standards.md](./universal/code-quality-standards.md) | P0 items pass, P1 items fixed or approved for deferral |
62: | 2 Debugging | [workflow-debug.md](./workflow-debug.md) | A named root cause and a fix that addresses that one cause |
63: | 3 Verification | [workflow-verify.md](./workflow-verify.md) | Fresh command output, exit codes and the delta from baseline |
64: 
65: `sk-code-review` runs outside this lifecycle. It writes no tracked file, so it has no Phase 1 and reports findings instead.
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. PER-SURFACE EVIDENCE
70: 
71: Surface precedence decides which table applies. `sk-code-skilled` is the fallback surface and is checked last. Any other surface that matches the task outranks it, including a private `local-*` surface skill where one is installed. When no surface matches, the surface is UNKNOWN and iron law 3 applies.
72: 
73: ### SKILLED (`sk-code-skilled`)
74: 
75: | Phase | Resources and evidence |
76: | --- | --- |
77: | 0 Research | `sk-code-skilled/references/shared/`, the affected skill, agent or command and the bound spec folder |
78: | 1 Implementation | `sk-code-skilled/references/shared/` plus the detected language folders from [stack-detection.md](./stack-detection.md) §3 |
79: | 1.5 Code Quality | `sk-code-skilled/assets/checklists/universal-checklist.md` plus the checklist for each touched language |
80: | 2 Debugging | Root-cause analysis, the failing command's output, language-specific patterns |
81: | 3 Verification | The drift-guard umbrella, plus targeted tests and spec validation |
82: 
83: The drift-guard umbrella runs four guards in one pass: alignment drift, stack folders, router sync and doc claims. It prints one PASS or FAIL line per guard and exits non-zero if any fails.
84: 
85: ```bash
86: bash .skilled/skills/sk-code/sk-code-skilled/scripts/run-all-drift-guards.sh
87: ```
88: 
89: ### CI (`sk-code-ci`)
90: 
91: | Phase | Resources and evidence |
92: | --- | --- |
93: | 0 Research | `sk-code-ci/references/protected-set.md`, then the workflow files the change touches |
94: | 1 Implementation | `sk-code-ci/assets/workflow-template.yml` or `job-block-template.yml`, plus the trigger, filter and job-shape rules |
95: | 1.5 Code Quality | The rule index in `sk-code-ci/references/ci-workflow-standards.md` |
96: | 2 Debugging | The failing workflow run and the rule it broke |
97: | 3 Verification | The machine gate the rule index names for each rule, plus a reviewer read for every honour-system rule |
98: 
99: The CI surface writes nothing. The acting agent applies its rules, and a rule the index marks honour-system has no check behind it, so only a careful read catches a lapse.
100: 
101: ### Frontend (`sk-code-frontend`)
102: 
103: | Phase | Resources and evidence |
104: | --- | --- |
105: | 0 Research | `sk-code-frontend/references/frontend-practice.md`, then the markup, style or component files the change touches and the design it must match |
106: | 1 Implementation | The same core, then `sk-code-frontend/references/web-markup-and-css.md`, then the one `web-*.md` topic file whose condition in the surface router applies |
107: | 1.5 Code Quality | The surface carries no checklist, so the gate stays with `sk-code-quality` and its universal floor |
108: | 2 Debugging | Root-cause analysis, the failing command's output and the stack layer or topic file that owns the behavior |
109: | 3 Verification | `sk-code-frontend/references/figma-to-code.md` where a built screen is compared with its Figma frame, plus the repository's own commands for that stack |
110: 
111: The Frontend surface writes nothing either. The acting mode applies its guidance, and a Figma pass that cannot run is marked `NOT RUN` with its reason, so the overall verdict is `INCOMPLETE`.
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 4. IRON LAWS
116: 
117: These hold on every surface and in every mode. No phase transition relaxes them.
118: 
119: 1. **No completion claim without Phase 3 verification evidence.** A clean read, a green unit test or a successful build each prove less than the claim "it works", so only fresh verification output counts.
120: 2. **No Phase 1 completion claim without the Phase 1.5 quality gate.** Written code is unreviewed code until its P0 items pass.
121: 3. **No claim about an unsupported surface.** An UNKNOWN surface gets:
122:    - the universal floor in [code-quality-standards.md](./universal/code-quality-standards.md),
123:    - the quality runner's built-in checks,
124:    - the checks and checklists the repository's quality config names,
125:    - each with its overrides applied under [rule-overrides.md](./universal/rule-overrides.md).
126: 
127:    That config can come from `--config`, the git config key `skcode.qualityConfig` or `repository/quality.json` in the `sk-code-quality` packet, and it never supplies a verification command, so the command set still comes from [workflow-verify.md](./workflow-verify.md), which asks for it. The spec-folder authoring checklist applies only where the SKILLED surface resolves. No other standard and no discovered command applies.
128: 
129: ---
130: 
131: ## 5. TRANSITIONS
132: 
133: | From | To | Condition |
134: | --- | --- | --- |
135: | 0 | 1 | Enough context and a plan exist. For implementation intent, the Phase 0 to 1 gate also requires choosing the laziest viable rung of the Design Restraint Ladder in [code-quality-standards.md](./universal/code-quality-standards.md) before any new code |
136: | 1 | 1.5 | Code was written or changed |
137: | 1.5 | 2 | A P0 quality issue or a failing check was found |
138: | 2 | 1.5 | A fix was applied, so the gate runs again on the changed code |
139: | 1.5 | 3 | Every P0 item passes, and each P1 item is fixed or approved for deferral |
140: | 3 | 1 | Verification finds required behavior missing or build work incomplete |
141: | 3 | 1.5 | An author-side check, comment hygiene or a checklist issue blocks verification |
142: | 3 | 2 | A command, runtime check or test fails, or a test proves nothing |
143: | 3 | done | Verification evidence is recorded |
144: 
145: ---
146: 
147: ## 6. RELATED RESOURCES
148: 
149: - [ROUTER.md](../../ROUTER.md) maps intent to resources and declares this file part of the always-loaded preamble.
150: - [stack-detection.md](./stack-detection.md) covers surface detection and SKILLED language sub-detection.
151: - [`../../sk-code-quality/SKILL.md`](../../sk-code-quality/SKILL.md) runs the Phase 1.5 gate.
152: - [`../../sk-code-ci/SKILL.md`](../../sk-code-ci/SKILL.md) holds the CI rule evidence and the protected set.
153: - [`../../sk-code-frontend/SKILL.md`](../../sk-code-frontend/SKILL.md) holds the frontend core, the web stack layer and the Figma-to-code check.

14: # Workflow Reference - Debugging
15: 
16: Shared `sk-code` doctrine for root-cause diagnosis and scoped repair once a symptom, failing command or failed check appears.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose
23: 
24: Debugging is the controlled-experiment phase. It reproduces or tightly characterizes the symptom, captures exact evidence, traces the symptom back to its source, fixes one cause at a time and sends the result back through quality and verification.
25: 
26: ### When to Use
27: 
28: - Diagnosing a failing test, build failure, runtime exception, console error, broken interaction, output regression, command failure or inconsistent runtime behavior.

14: # Router Reference - Code Surface Detection
15: 
16: `sk-code` detects the code surface before it classifies intent. It reads the working directory and the changed or target files, because one repository can hold the hub's own code beside another stack.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose
23: 
24: This reference gives one detection contract that every sk-code reader applies before it classifies intent, so each route loads the resources of the surface the work actually touches.
25: 
26: ### When to Use
27: 
28: - Before intent classification, when the request's surface is not yet settled
29: - When a specific surface and SKILLED both match and their order decides which resources load
30: - When a hub surface's `surfaceDetection` block or an external skill's `surface_detection` block is declared or checked
31: 
32: ### Core Principle
33: 
34: Detect **where the work is happening** before deciding which standards apply. The narrowest declared surface that matches leads, and the hub's own code comes last.
35: 
36: ### Surfaces
37: 
38: | Surface | Owns | Does Not Own |
39: | --- | --- | --- |
40: | Specific surfaces | The stack each one declares, such as an operator-private `local-*` skill or a surface packet another repository adds to the hub | Work that matches none of their markers |
41: | SKILLED | The hub's own code under `.skilled/`: skills, agents, commands, MCP servers, plugins, scripts, tests and JSON or YAML config. It is the one fallback surface | A stack a specific surface declares |
42: | UNKNOWN | The result when no declared surface matches | Any standard beyond the universal floor, the quality runner's built-in checks and the checks and checklists the repository's quality config names, each with its overrides applied, until the operator names the surface and its commands. The spec-folder authoring checklist needs the SKILLED surface |
43: 
44: `sk-code-ci` and `sk-code-frontend` are surface packets with no detection block. The hub bundles each from request vocabulary alone, so detection never returns either.
45: 
46: ---
47: 
48: ## 2. DETECTION ORDER
49: 
50: ### The Rule
51: 
52: When a specific surface and SKILLED both match, the specific surface leads and SKILLED stays as second evidence. Every reader takes the order from the declarations below, so no implementation keeps a list of its own:
53: 
54: ```text
55: 1. The hub's own specific surfaces, in modes[] order in mode-registry.json.
56: 2. Specific surfaces that skills outside the hub declare, sorted by skill_id.
57: 3. SKILLED, the fallback. It leads only when no specific surface matched.
58:    Otherwise it follows them as second evidence and is never dropped.
59: 4. UNKNOWN when nothing matched. Apply the universal floor, the quality runner's built-in checks and the checks and checklists the repository's quality config names, each with its overrides applied under `universal/rule-overrides.md`. The spec-folder authoring checklist needs the SKILLED surface, no discovered command applies, and the operator is asked which surface and which commands apply.
60: ```
61: 
62: ### Why SKILLED Is Last
63: 
64: A specific surface names one stack exactly. SKILLED is the hub's own code and the broadest surface, and one task can touch hub files beside another stack. If the broad surface came first, it would hide the narrow one. Keeping SKILLED as second evidence still loads its standards for the hub files the task touches.
65: 
66: The registry compiler enforces the order on every compile. It fails with `SURFACE_FALLBACK_INVALID` unless the hub declares exactly one fallback and ranks it last in `routerPolicy.tieBreak` in `hub-router.json`, so a keyword tie between specific surfaces also ranks SKILLED last. The compiled router ignores `--surface-hint SKILLED` for the same reason. A hinted specific surface takes the first surface slot only when the prompt matched it.
67: 
68: ### Declaring a Hub Surface
69: 
70: Each surface entry in `mode-registry.json` may carry a `surfaceDetection` block. The SKILLED block reads:
71: 
72: ```json
73: "surfaceDetection": {
74:   "label": "SKILLED",
75:   "role": "fallback",
76:   "pathMarkers": [".skilled/", ".opencode/"],
77:   "fileMarkers": ["SKILL.md", ".ts", ".tsx", ".cjs", ".mjs", ".py", ".sh", ".rs"],
78:   "contentMarkers": ["graph-metadata", "spec-folder", "argparse"]
79: }
80: ```
81: 
82: - `label` is the surface name detection reports and the value `--surface-hint` carries. Readers compare it in upper case.
83: - `role` is `specific` or `fallback`.
84: - `pathMarkers` are path segments, such as the folder a surface lives in.
85: - `fileMarkers` are file names or extensions.
86: - `contentMarkers` are text found in a touched file or in the request.
87: 
88: The compiler fails with `SURFACE_DETECTION_INVALID` when a block sits on a mode that is not a surface, names another role, declares no marker or reuses another block's label. A missing or empty label, or a marker that is not a string, fails with `AUTHORED_INPUT_INVALID`.
89: 
90: ### Declaring an External Surface
91: 
92: A skill outside the hub declares the same block under the top-level key `surface_detection` in its own `graph-metadata.json`. The skill sits beside the hub in `.skilled/skills/` and names `"family": "sk-code"`. A skill named `local-example`, for example, could declare:
93: 
94: ```json
95: {
96:   "skill_id": "local-example",
97:   "family": "sk-code",
98:   "surface_detection": {
99:     "label": "EXAMPLE",
100:     "role": "specific",
101:     "pathMarkers": ["src/example/"],
102:     "contentMarkers": ["example-marker"]
103:   }
104: }
105: ```
106: 
107: These rules apply to an external block:
108: 
109: - It must state `"role": "specific"`. Readers ignore a block that claims the fallback role or states no role, because the fallback is the hub's own code.
110: - It needs a label and at least one marker, or it never matches.
111: - The registry compiler reads only the hub's registry, so it never checks the inner fields. Pick markers that do not catch other repositories. A bare `manifest.json` file marker would.
112: - The skill-root metadata check, `ci-skill-root-metadata.cjs`, accepts `surface_detection` as an optional top-level key and checks its fields. It fails with `GRAPH_METADATA_INVALID_SURFACE_DETECTION`, one finding per broken rule, when:
113:   - the value is not a JSON object,
114:   - the `label` is missing or blank,
115:   - the `role` is anything but `specific`,
116:   - none of `pathMarkers`, `fileMarkers` and `contentMarkers` is a non-empty array, or
117:   - one of those three is present but is not an array of strings.
118: 
119:   A marker must not be blank: one made only of spaces or tabs fails, because it would match nearly every path or request.
120: - The check skips folders whose name starts with `local-`, so it does not validate a private skill such as `local-example`. Check that block by hand against the rules above.
121: 
122: ### The Fallback and the Symlink Guard
123: 
124: SKILLED is the hub's own code. On real file paths it holds only through its path markers, and only when the resolved path lands inside the hub's own `.skilled/` folder, or inside the folder its plugins link resolves to when that folder is not an ancestor of the hub. Its file and content markers serve text-only detection, such as a router replay over request text that has no resolved paths. Without that limit, the `.ts` marker would make a TypeScript file in any repository SKILLED.
125: 
126: Resolve symlinks before testing. A downstream plugin repository symlinks `.opencode`, `.claude`, `.codex`, `.cursor` and `.devin` at its root back to this hub. An operator's private `local-*` skills sit in the hub's `.skilled/skills/` folder as symlinks to another repository. A literal test for a `.skilled/` or `.opencode/` segment would therefore report SKILLED for work that never touches a hub file. After the paths resolve:
127: 
128: - A genuine hub file reached through a symlink, such as `.opencode/agents/code.md`, is SKILLED.
129: - A file that belongs to the downstream repository is not SKILLED, whatever its path string says.
130: - A file inside a symlinked `local-*` skill is not SKILLED, because it resolves to another repository.
131: 
132: The guard changes how the test runs, not the order.
133: 
134: ### Where Detection Runs
135: 
136: Each reader applies this contract to the input it has:
137: 
138: | Reader | Input | A specific surface matches on | SKILLED matches on | Returns |
139: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
140: | `detectWorkspaceSurface` in `.opencode/plugins/system-skill-advisor.js` | The resolved working directory | A path marker the directory holds or sits inside, or a file marker naming a file in it. Extension and content markers are skipped | The directory lying inside the hub's own `.skilled/` | The first match as the session's `--surface-hint`, or no hint |
141: | `detectSurfaces` in `sk-code-skilled/assets/scripts/router-replay-lib.cjs` | The request text only | Any marker found in the text | Any of its markers found in the text | Every matching label in order, with the first as the lead |
142: | `fileLabels` in `sk-code-quality/scripts/quality-gate.cjs` | Each changed file's resolved real path, name and content | A path marker on a path segment, a file marker on the extension or exact name, or a content marker in the text | Its path markers, only when the real path lies inside the hub's own `.skilled/` folder, or inside the folder its plugins link resolves to when that folder is not an ancestor of the hub | Each file's labels in order, or `UNKNOWN`, and their union for the run, or `unknown` |
143: | The resolver step in `sk-code-review/SKILL.md` | The reviewed files | It runs no detection of its own and reads each file's `surfaces` from `quality-gate.cjs --explain`, the `fileLabels` row above | The same as `fileLabels` | Each file's labels in order, or `UNKNOWN` |
144: 
145: ---
146: 
147: ## 3. SKILLED LANGUAGE SUB-DETECTION
148: 
149: Whenever SKILLED is detected, as the leading surface or as second evidence, select language resources by extension first:
150: 
151: | Language | Extensions | Resource Folder |
152: | --- | --- | --- |
153: | JAVASCRIPT | `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs` | `sk-code-skilled/references/javascript/` |
154: | TYPESCRIPT | `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.mts`, `.d.ts` | `sk-code-skilled/references/typescript/` |
155: | PYTHON | `.py` | `sk-code-skilled/references/python/` |
156: | SHELL | `.sh`, `.bash` | `sk-code-skilled/references/shell/` |
157: | RUST | `.rs`, then the `Cargo.toml` or `Cargo.lock` markers and napi-rs or wasm-bindgen vocabulary | `sk-code-skilled/references/rust/` |
158: | CONFIG | `.json`, `.jsonc`, `.yaml`, `.yml` | `sk-code-skilled/references/config/` |
159: 
160: When a task touches more than one language, load the shared guidance in `sk-code-skilled/references/shared/` plus the quick reference and checklist of each touched language.
161: 
162: Rust never overrides another language. A napi-rs or WASM parity task that touches `.rs` and `.ts` loads both trios plus the shared guidance, because the Rust module must match its TypeScript oracle byte for byte. The Cargo markers count only after SKILLED is detected, never as a signal for another project's surface.
163: 
164: YAML is live hub config: command routers, workflow contracts and each command's auto and confirm assets.
165: 
166: ---
167: 
168: ## 4. TEST CASES
169: 
170: | Context | Expected Surface | Reason |
171: | --- | --- | --- |
172: | CWD `.skilled/skills/sk-code` | SKILLED | The directory resolves inside the hub's own `.skilled/` |
173: | Changed `.skilled/agents/code.md` | SKILLED | The target file is under `.skilled/` |
174: | Literal path string contains `.opencode/` but resolves outside the hub | Not SKILLED | The symlink guard refuses SKILLED on a string match alone |
175: | Changed file inside a symlinked `.skilled/skills/local-*` skill | Not SKILLED | The file resolves to another repository |
176: | Changed `src/2_javascript/slider.js`, with a declared specific surface naming `src/2_javascript/` | That surface | A declared specific surface outranks the fallback |
177: | Changed `src/2_javascript/slider.js` and `.opencode/agents/code.md`, with a declared specific surface naming `src/2_javascript/` | **That surface**, then SKILLED as second evidence | Specific surfaces lead, and the fallback still loads for the hub file |
178: | Changed `apps/desktop/src/styles/app.css` and `.opencode/agents/code.md`, with no specific surface declared | SKILLED | The fallback is the only declared surface that matches |
179: | Router replay of request text naming `.skilled/skills/x/foo.ts` | SKILLED | Text-only detection matches the fallback's markers in the request |
180: | A prompt that bundles SKILLED and CI, sent with `--surface-hint SKILLED` | CI first, then SKILLED | A hint that names the fallback never moves it ahead of another surface |
181: | Root `package.json` with no `.skilled/` target | UNKNOWN | No declared surface owns generic Node.js |
182: | `go.mod` or `next.config.js` only | UNKNOWN | No declared surface names Go or Next.js |
183: 
184: ---
185: 
186: ## 5. RELATED RESOURCES
187: 
188: - [`../../mode-registry.json`](../../mode-registry.json): the `surfaceDetection` blocks and the `surface-axis` contract text.
189: - [`../../hub-router.json`](../../hub-router.json): `routerPolicy.tieBreak`, which ranks the fallback last.
190: - [`../../ROUTER.md`](../../ROUTER.md): root intent classification, resource maps, declared shared controls and load tiers.
191: - [`./phase-detection.md`](./phase-detection.md): the Phase 1, 2 and 3 lifecycle and per-phase resource loading.
192: - `ROUTER.md` section 11: the compiled-routing directive, including the session surface hint.

15: # Rule Overrides Contract
16: 
17: How a repository or a surface drops or replaces a sk-code rule, and which rules no one can change.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: Each repository keeps its own house style. One wants almost no inline comments, and another wants a comment on every function. The quality mode and the review mode ship default rules, and this contract is how a repository or a surface says "not here" or "this instead" for one of them. Both modes read the same section in the same files, so a rule dropped for quality does not come back as a review finding.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - A repository or surface needs to drop or replace a rule outside the hard floor.
30: - A checklist needs a `## Rule overrides` section, or a mode needs to know how one is read and recorded.
31: 
32: ### Core Principle
33: 
34: A repository may change any rule except the hard floor. The floor holds the rules whose breach causes an incident in any codebase, and the review severity scale that every finding is ranked on.
35: 
36: ### Scope
37: 
38: This file defines the format, the ids, the floor, the precedence and how an applied override is recorded.
39: 
40: - The quality and review modes adopt it in their own contracts.
41: - The review mode applies the rows it reads and records them on its `Rule sources` line.
42: - The quality runner reads the section of every checklist it loads through the same linter, applies and records the rows as section 7 describes, and shows the parsed rows and the conflicts in its explain output.
43: - Its registry of known rule ids is read from the documents that declare them, and `commentHygiene.disableRules` carries the machine-checked half.
44: - A mode that does not state that it reads overrides behaves as before.
45: 
46: ### Key Sources
47: 
48: - [`rule-overrides.json`](./rule-overrides.json): the machine-readable hard floor and the machine-checked classes. The linter reads it, and sections 2 and 4 of this file mirror it.
49: - [`../../scripts/check-rule-overrides.cjs`](../../scripts/check-rule-overrides.cjs): the linter that checks a section.
50: - [`../../scripts/lib/rule-registry.cjs`](../../scripts/lib/rule-registry.cjs): the registry of rule ids the quality runner checks a row's id against.
51: - [`../../../sk-code-quality/references/runner-contract.md`](../../../sk-code-quality/references/runner-contract.md) section 5: the `<class>.<name>` rule id grammar this contract reuses.
52: 
53: ---
54: 
55: ## 2. THE SECTION AND ITS ROWS
56: 
57: An override lives in an optional section of a checklist file. The heading reads `## Rule overrides`. A checklist that numbers its headings in upper case may write `## 7. RULE OVERRIDES`, and the linter reads both. The section runs to the next H1 or H2 heading. A file carries at most one.
58: 
59: The section holds one table with three columns:
60: 
61: ```markdown
62: ## Rule overrides
63: 
64: | Rule | Action | Reason |
65: | --- | --- | --- |
66: | `floor.documentation` | none | Public functions carry no doc comments here |
67: | `review.function-length` | replace: A function stays under 60 lines | The team's own limit |
68: ```
69: 
70: | Column | Required | Meaning |
71: | --- | --- | --- |
72: | Rule | Yes | One rule id from section 3. Backticks are optional |
73: | Action | Yes | `none` drops the rule. `replace: <text>` puts the text in its place, with the same severity |
74: | Reason | No | Why the repository differs. A reviewer reads it when the override is recorded |
75: 
76: A row names a single rule, and a section names each rule once. Write a literal pipe in the replacement text as `\|`. Prose lines and fenced examples inside the section are ignored.
77: 
78: A row for a machine-checked id (`hygiene.*`, `debug.*`, `dist.*`) changes what the agent and review apply. The runner's own check changes only through `commentHygiene.disableRules` in the repository's quality config. A `replace:` row on a machine-checked id is refused, because no row can rewrite what the runner matches.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: ## 3. RULE IDS
83: 
84: A rule id is `<class>.<name>`, the grammar of `runner-contract.md` section 5. The class and the name are lower case, and each takes letters, digits and hyphens.
85: 
86: | Class | Names | Source |
87: | --- | --- | --- |
88: | `hygiene`, `conflict`, `secret`, `syntax`, `debug`, `dist` | The runner's own rule names, such as `hygiene.task` | `runner-contract.md` section 5 |
89: | `floor` | One per rule in the universal standards, such as `floor.input-validation` | `code-quality-standards.md` sections 3 to 5 |
90: | `review` | One per rule in the review default lens, such as `review.function-length` | The sk-code-review mode |
91: 
92: A row names a concrete id. A wildcard such as `hygiene.*` is not a row id. The linter checks the grammar, the action and the floor, not whether the id names a rule that exists. Section 7 says what a mode does with an unknown id.
93: 
94: A review check that enforces a rule of the universal floor carries that rule's `floor.*` id, never a `review.*` id, so an override written for the review lens cannot reach a floor rule.
95: 
96: ---
97: 
98: ## 4. THE HARD FLOOR
99: 
100: These ids are fixed. A section that names one is refused. An id ending in `.*` fixes every rule in that class, so a parse rule added later is fixed from the start.
101: 
102: | Id | Rule |
103: | --- | --- |
104: | `syntax.*` | Parse failure: the file does not parse in its language |
105: | `conflict.*` | Merge-conflict markers left in a text file |
106: | `secret.*` | Credential signature: a private-key header or a token in a known format |
107: | `floor.hardcoded-secrets` | No hardcoded secrets: credentials come from the environment or a secret store |
108: | `floor.input-validation` | Input validation: every external input is validated at the boundary |
109: | `floor.silent-failures` | No silent failures: an error reaches the caller or is logged with context |
110: | `floor.initialization-safety` | Initialization safety: setup guards against double init, races and partial loads |
111: | `floor.resource-cleanup` | Resource cleanup: handles, connections, subscriptions and timers close deterministically |
112: | `floor.accessibility` | Accessibility for UI code: keyboard-operable, an accessible name and a visible focus state |
113: | `review.severity` | The review severity ids P0, P1 and P2 and what each one means |
114: | `review.reach` | The review reach rule: a P0 or P1 finding names an input or caller in reach |
115: | `review.security-minimums` | Review security minimums: auth and authorization gaps, injection exposure, unsafe secrets handling and privilege misuse |
116: | `review.correctness-minimums` | Review correctness minimums: regression risk, contract safety, spec mismatch, destructive side effects and boundary handling |
117: 
118: The four `review.*` ids fix the floor of [`review-core.md`](../../../sk-code-review/references/review-core.md): its severity ids and reach rule in section 2, and the baseline security and correctness minimums in sections 5 and 6, which that file says surface guidance cannot relax.
119: 
120: Every other rule can be overridden. That covers comment hygiene, documentation, typing strictness, naming, commented-out code, the `ceiling:` marker and every P2 rule. The list above and [`rule-overrides.json`](./rule-overrides.json) hold the same ids, and a test fails when they differ.
121: 
122: ---
123: 
124: ## 5. PRECEDENCE
125: 
126: When more than one source speaks to the same rule for a file, the higher level wins:
127: 
128: 1. **The hard floor.** No source changes it.
129: 2. **The repository checklist.** A file named in `checklists[]` of the repository's quality config, `repository/quality.json` in the `sk-code-quality` packet.
130: 3. **A specific surface.** A hub surface other than SKILLED, or an outside skill that declares a surface.
131: 4. **The SKILLED fallback.** The `sk-code-skilled` checklists.
132: 5. **The default lens.** The rule as the mode ships it.
133: 
134: Two sources at the same level that disagree on one rule for one file are a conflict, and section 7 says how each mode handles it. Two sources that give the same action and the same text agree, and that is no conflict.
135: 
136: ---
137: 
138: ## 6. WHERE A SECTION MAY LIVE
139: 
140: A section has effect only in a checklist file that an existing declaration already names. A mode never searches for override sections elsewhere.
141: 
142: | Seat | Declared in | Level |
143: | --- | --- | --- |
144: | A hub surface checklist | That surface's `quality.checklists` in the hub's `mode-registry.json` | Specific surface, or the SKILLED fallback for `sk-code-skilled` |
145: | An outside skill checklist | The `quality` block beside `surface_detection` in that skill's `graph-metadata.json` | Specific surface |
146: | A repository checklist | `checklists[]` in `repository/quality.json`, the `sk-code-quality` packet's quality config | Repository |
147: 
148: A checklist applies to the files its declaration matches by path or extension, and so does its section. An override in a checklist for `.github/workflows/**` never reaches a Python file.
149: 
150: ---
151: 
152: ## 7. READING AND RECORDING AN OVERRIDE
153: 
154: A mode reads a section only through `lintOverrides` in the linter, the same code the command line runs. An override is a judgment the reader must be able to see, so every outcome is recorded where the mode already records its judgment.
155: 
156: | Outcome | Quality | Review |
157: | --- | --- | --- |
158: | A valid row, the highest source for its rule | Applies it and records `override <rule id> <none\|replace> from <checklist file>` in the envelope's `p0_p1_p2_decisions` | Applies it and lists it under `Overrides` on the `Rule sources` line |
159: | `lintOverrides` returns any error for a file | Applies none of that file's overrides and reports the file as `CONFIG_INVALID`, exit 3 | Applies none of that file's overrides and lists the file under `Refused` |
160: | A row names an id no rule carries | Refuses the file as `CONFIG_INVALID`, exit 3 | Ignores the row and lists it under `Ignored` |
161: | Two sources at the same level disagree on one rule | Records `override-conflict <rule id> <file> <file>` in `p0_p1_p2_decisions`, keeps the default for that rule and reports the rule as unverified, with no new exit code | Applies the default and lists the rule under `Conflicts` |
162: 
163: The review report carries one `Rule sources` line. It lists the checklist files the review read, then each outcome group, and writes `none` for an empty group:
164: 
165: ```text
166: Rule sources: <checklist file>, <checklist file>. Overrides: <rule id> none from <checklist file>. Refused: none. Ignored: none. Conflicts: none
167: ```
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 8. CHECKING A SECTION
172: 
173: Run the linter on a checklist file before a declaration names it:
174: 
175: ```bash
176: node .skilled/skills/sk-code/shared/scripts/check-rule-overrides.cjs <checklist.md> [<checklist.md>...]
177: ```
178: 
179: | Exit | Meaning |
180: | --- | --- |
181: | 0 | Every file has a valid section or none |
182: | 1 | A row is refused: a floor id, a `replace:` row on a machine-checked id, an unknown action, a malformed row or id, a repeated id or a second section. Each problem prints as `<file>:<line>: <message>` |
183: | 2 | A usage error, an unreadable file or an unreadable contract file |
184: 
185: The linter exports `lintOverrides`, `loadContract` and `RULE_ID`, the id grammar, so a reader that checks an id outside a section uses the same pattern. `lintOverrides(text)` returns the accepted rows and every error, and a mode applies the rows only when the error list is empty.
186: 
187: ---
188: 
189: ## 9. RELATED RESOURCES
190: 
191: - [`code-quality-standards.md`](./code-quality-standards.md): the universal floor and its P0, P1 and P2 tiers.
192: - [`../../../sk-code-review/references/review-core.md`](../../../sk-code-review/references/review-core.md): the review severity ids, the reach rule and the baseline minimums that this contract fixes.
193: - [`../../../sk-code-quality/references/runner-contract.md`](../../../sk-code-quality/references/runner-contract.md): the runner's rule ids and its envelope.

38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95: 
96: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
97: 
98: ```markdown
99: # Git Commit Workflows
100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131:

134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.

202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```
229: 
230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766:

769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"

789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1

796:     enable_feature_x: true

798:     $quick: "quick_mode"

800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible

884: 
885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass
1006:

1009: ## 8. STANDARD STRUCTURE TEMPLATE
1010: 
1011: ### Complete Skill Directory Structure
1012: 
1013: **Path:** `.skilled/skills/` (singular, not `skills` or `openskills`)
1014: 
1015: ```
1016: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
1017: ├── SKILL.md                    # Main skill file (Level 2 in progressive disclosure)
1018: ├── references/                 # Deep-dive technical documentation (Level 3)
1019: │   ├── workflow-name.md        # Multi-phase workflows with checkpoints (kebab-case)
1020: │   ├── patterns-library.md     # Before/after code patterns (kebab-case)
1021: │   ├── debugging-guide.md      # Systematic troubleshooting (kebab-case)
1022: │   └── quick-reference.md      # Commands, shortcuts, checklists (kebab-case)
1023: ├── scripts/                    # Executable Python logic
1024: │   ├── mode_detection.py       # Procedural logic, algorithms
1025: │   ├── workflow_router.py      # Decision logic
1026: │   ├── config_validator.py     # Data transformation
1027: │   └── __init__.py             # Package initialization
1028: ├── assets/                     # Configuration and data files
1029: │   ├── workflow-configs/       # YAML workflow definitions
1030: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
1031: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
1032: │   ├── mappings/               # YAML mapping data
1033: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
1034: │   │   └── mode-recognition.yaml
1035: │   └── templates/              # Markdown/code templates
1036: │       ├── template-name.md
1037: │       └── component-template.tsx
1038: └── tests/                      # Unit and integration tests
1039:     ├── test_mode_detection.py
1040:     ├── test_workflow_router.py
1041:     ├── test_config_validator.py
1042:     └── __init__.py
1043: ```
1044: 
1045: ### Directory Purposes
1046: 
1047: **SKILL.md** (Required): Overview, workflow (3-5 steps), rules. Target: <200 lines
1048: 
1049: **references/** (Optional): Detailed workflows, patterns, debugging. Target: 500-3000 lines/file. **All authored filenames must use kebab-case.**
1050: 
1051: **scripts/** (Optional): Python logic - procedural, routing, validation. Requires type hints, tests
1052: 
1053: **assets/** (Optional): YAML configs, workflow definitions, templates, mappings
1054: 
1055: **tests/** (Required if scripts/ exists): Unit tests with ≥80% coverage, pytest, `test_[name].py`
1056: 
1057: ### When to Create Each Directory
1058: 
1059: | Directory     | Create When                                                     | Don't Create When                           |
1060: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
1061: | `references/` | Content >200 lines, multi-phase workflows, systematic debugging | Simple skills <200 lines total              |
1062: | `scripts/`    | Python logic extracted from markdown, reusable functions        | Pure documentation, no executable logic     |
1063: | `assets/`     | YAML configs, templates, structured data                        | No configuration data, inline examples only |
1064: | `tests/`      | `scripts/` directory exists                                     | No Python scripts to test                   |
1065: 
1066: ### Integration Pattern
1067: 
1068: **How components work together:**
1069: - SKILL.md references scripts: `[workflow_router.py](./scripts/workflow_router.py)`
1070: - Scripts load configs: `yaml.safe_load(f"../assets/config.yaml")`
1071: - Tests verify scripts: `assert route_workflow("input").mode == "expected"`
1072: - Markdown links to all: "See [script.py](../scripts/), [config.yaml](../assets/)"

14: # Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills
15: 
16: Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Location & Naming
23: 
24: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`
25: 
26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only
27: 
28: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
29: |---------------|-----------------|
30: | `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
31: | `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
32: | `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
33: | `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |
34: | `code-quality-standards.md` | `code quality standards.md` (spaces) |
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95: 
96: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
97: 
98: ```markdown
99: # Git Commit Workflows
100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.
199:
